content.title: About
content.content: Lobster is a crustacean marine product found in cold coastal waters of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Its meat is tender, slightly sweet, and carries a distinct sea flavor. Lobster is commonly served boiled, baked, or as a gourmet dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lobsters can change the color of their shells depending on the environment and mood.
An adult lobster can live over 50 years and reach weights of more than 20 kg.
Lobsters can regenerate lost claws and legs.
The largest recorded lobster weighed over 20 kg and was caught off the coast of Canada.
Lobsters use their powerful claws not only for hunting but also for communication.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Lobster meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafoods, lobster contains very little fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support the immune system and have antioxidant properties.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Lobster supplies vitamin B12, important for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: A modest amount of omega‑3 contributes to heart and vascular health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to lobster.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Lobster contains cholesterol, so people with elevated cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Toxic organs
items.content: The tomalley and hepatopancreas can accumulate toxins and are usually not eaten.

items.title: Risk of overconsumption
items.content: Because lobster is expensive, diners may eat large portions, leading to excess sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lobster is typically boiled in salted water for 8–12 minutes, then served with melted butter, lemon, or a sauce. The meat is removed from the claws and tail and can be added to salads, pastas, risottos, or served as a hot appetizer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep live lobster on ice in the refrigerator, covered with a damp cloth, for up to 2 days. Frozen lobster should be stored at –18 °C and used within 3–4 months. Thaw frozen lobster in the refrigerator before cooking.
